summary: This standards-track RFC describes a way to electronically sign Routing Policy Specification Language objects and validate the signatures, using RPKI. Relying parties can detect accidental or malicious modification, and registries lacking maintainer authentication gain a way to establish it.

eli5.summary: Putting a tamper-proof seal on routing registry entries so anyone can tell if they were changed.

questions: what is the rpsl signature attribute
how does rpki secure routing registry objects
subtitle: Signing routing registry objects with RPKI certificates so anyone can check who made them and whether they were altered.

tldr.problem: Routing registry objects copied between databases lose their authentication guarantees, and once downloaded they are plain text with no integrity protection.
tldr.mechanism: The holder of Internet number resources adds a new signature attribute, made with the private key of an RPKI resource certificate over a canonicalized form of chosen attributes. Anyone can then validate it against the certificate.
tldr.outcome: Users of an object can verify that it was produced by the legitimate holder of the resources it mentions, wherever the object is hosted. One limitation is that only a single signature per object is supported.

facts.label: Signature attribute fields
facts.value: 6 mandatory (v, c, m, t, a, b), 1 optional (x)

today: RFC 7909 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2016. It has not been obsoleted and it updates RFC 2622 and RFC 4012 by adding the signature attribute to supported RPSL objects.

sections.title: The Problem and the Idea
sections.content:
Objects in resource databases such as the RIPE DB are normally protected by authentication when someone creates or changes them. That guarantee does not carry over when objects are transferred between databases. A consumer can reasonably trust an object created locally, but not one imported from elsewhere. After download, an object is just a structured text file with no integrity protection.

RFC 7909 proposes using resource certificates (RFC 6487) to secure such Routing Policy Specification Language (RPSL) objects with a digital signature, instead of methods such as Routing Policy System Security (RFC 2725). The signer MUST hold a relevant resource certificate that shows them as the legitimate holder of an Internet number resource. This gives object security on top of the channel security most databases already have, so signed objects can be hosted in different databases and still be verified independently.

The approach mandates RPKI for certificate distribution but does not depend on it to work. A more traditional CA using the RFC 3779 extensions would give equivalent functionality.
sections.eli5: When a note is copied from one notebook to another, nobody can tell who really wrote it. A signature that travels with the note fixes that.

sections.title: The Signature Attribute
sections.content:
The signature is itself a new attribute named signature. Its value is a sequence of name and value pairs separated by a semicolon and a whitespace. Each name is a single ASCII character. Mandatory fields appear exactly once and optional fields at most once. The approach is adapted from DKIM (RFC 6376), because an RPSL object closely resembles an SMTP header.

  • v: version, which MUST be rpkiv1.
  • c: URL (rsync or http(s)) of the resource certificate whose private key signed the object.
  • m: hash and signature algorithms, following RFC 6485.
  • t: time of signing, in Internet Date/Time format converted to UTC.
  • a: the signed attribute names, joined with +, each at most once.
  • b: the signature in base64, which MUST be the last field.
  • x (optional): expiration time, also in UTC.

The result of signing is exactly one new attribute appended to the object. The signature is valid for the intersection of the certificate's validity, the t time as a not-before, and the optional x time as a not-after.
sections.eli5: The signature is one extra line at the bottom of the entry. It says who signed, which lines were covered, when, and carries the secret-pen mark itself.

sections.title: Creating and Validating a Signature
sections.content:
To create a signature, the signer lists the attributes to sign, arranges them in that order, builds the signature attribute with b left empty, canonicalizes the result, signs it with the algorithms named in m, puts the base64 value into b, and appends the attribute to the original object.

To validate, a verifier checks the attribute's syntax, fetches the certificate named in c and checks it per RFC 6487, and reads the signed list from a. It confirms the list includes the minimum set for the object type, rebuilds the same ordered view with b emptied, canonicalizes it, and checks the signature with the public key from the certificate.

If the attribute list is incomplete, the verifier MUST reject the signature and treat the object as a regular, unsigned RPSL object. The certificate's RFC 3779 resources must also cover the resources in the object's primary key, such as aut-num, inetnum, or route and origin.
sections.eli5: To check the letter, you rebuild the same summary the signer made and see if the signature fits. If anything differs, you treat the letter as unsigned.

sections.title: Canonicalization
sections.content:
Databases may rewrite objects after they were signed, for example by changing how prefixes are written, adding or modifying changed attributes, or using different line endings. Any such change would break a signature. RFC 7909 solves this with strict canonicalization rules applied before signing and before verifying.

  • Comments (anything starting with a hash character) and trailing whitespace are removed.
  • Multi-line attributes become a single line, ending in one newline.
  • Dates and times are UTC in Internet Date/Time format. AS numbers use ASPLAIN (RFC 5396), IPv6 addresses follow RFC 5952, and all prefixes use CIDR notation (RFC 4632).
  • Attribute names are lowercased, tabs become spaces, and runs of whitespace collapse to one space.
  • All line endings become a single newline, avoiding CR versus CRLF differences.

The order of values within list-style fields MUST be maintained during database transfers.
sections.eli5: Before signing, everyone first writes the entry in exactly the same neat style. That way a different tidy-up by another database cannot fool the check.

sections.title: Which Objects and Attributes Are Signed
sections.content:
Each object type has a minimum set of attributes that MUST be signed, and the signer MAY add more. The list excludes attributes used for referential integrity inside a database, such as mnt-by, admin-c and tech-c. The objects they point to can change without the signed object changing, so signing them could give a false sense of security.

  • as-block: as-block, signature.
  • aut-num: aut-num, as-name, member-of, the import, export and default attributes (including the mp- forms), signature.
  • inet[6]num: the number itself, netname, country, status, signature.
  • route[6]: the route, origin, holes, member-of, signature.

The certificate's RFC 3779 extension MUST include a resource entry equal to or less specific than the resource in the object. For a route object, that means the route or the origin or both. Only a single signature per object is supported, so a route[6] object cannot be properly signed when one holder owns the ASN and another owns the prefix.
sections.eli5: Each kind of entry has a list of lines that must be covered. Lines that just point to other entries are optional, because those other entries can change on their own.

sections.title: Certificates Used for Signing
sections.content:
The certificate referenced in the c field MUST be an end-entity (non-CA) certificate. It MUST conform to the X.509 PKIX Resource Certificate profile (RFC 6487). It MUST carry the RFC 3779 extension covering the Internet number resource in a signed attribute.

These certificates omit the Subject Information Access (SIA) extension that RFC 6487 would otherwise require. That extension needs an rsync URI, and RPSL does not currently support database access through rsync.
sections.eli5: The signing pen must belong to a real owner of the address space, and it must be a plain owner's pen, not one that hands out other pens.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RPSL objects in Internet Routing Registry databases are public, so confidentiality is not a goal. Each signed object has its integrity and authenticity checked with the signature and the referenced certificate. The security considerations of RFC 3779 also apply, and implementers MUST follow the certificate validation steps of RFC 6487.

A maintainer can include attributes in the signature that name resources the certificate does not cover, so a maintainer may reference resources they are not authorized to use. The signature also does not stop an in-the-middle adversary who removes the signature attribute, changes the contents, or drops the objects.
sections.eli5: The signature shows a note was not changed, but it cannot stop someone from tearing off the signature or hiding the note.
